newsitem.title: USA: Good news about saving for retirement.
newsitem.headline: Good news about saving for retirement.

text.p: Forget, for a few moments, the gloom-and-doom financial diet most pre-retirees are put on.
If you had a nickel for every time someone said "you're not saving enough," you'd probably be able to retire rich and not have to save another penny.
But now there's some encouraging news on the retirement savings front.
According to new research by Baltimore mutual fund company T. Rowe Price, most retirement planning programmes vastly overestimate the income tax rate to which post-retirement income is subjected.
The typical retirement planning exercise requires you to figure out how much you can take out of your IRA for twenty years, for example, and then have to reduce that by your marginal tax rate.

So if you are in the marginal 28 percent tax bracket with a 5 percent state tax, and you can afford to take $500 a month out of your IRA, you'll be left with $335 a month after taxes. If you needed $500 a month in the first place, you'd have to take out $746 a month just to net $500 after taxes, these programmes tell you.

That typically means that you run out of money faster, or that you need to save far more money in your working years to make sure you can cover the tax bills as well as the condo fees once you hang up your briefcase.
But using new figures calculated by the Washington-based Tax Foundation, analysts at T. Rowe Price have discovered that the tax burden on most retirees is much lower than expected.

In the first place, using marginal tax rates to calculate these figures ignores that most money is not taxed at the marginal rate, but at a personal average income tax rate that is much lower. In addition, retirees receive a larger percent of their income on a tax-free basis: Their Social Security benefits are tax-free until total income rises above $32,000 for a married couple and $25,000 for single filers, and even at top tax brackets no more than 80 percent of these benefits are taxable.
The effect this has on taxes in retirement can be sizable.

Take a well-off couple earning $35,000 in dividends and interest and $19,200 in Social Security benefits, for a total of $54,900. If this couple takes the standard deduction, their annual income tax will be $3,364, or 6.2 percent of their gross income, even though their income puts them squarely in the 28 percent marginal tax bracket.

What if this couple then decides to withdraw $10,000 from an IRA account, subjecting it to income tax? They'd have to come up with an additional $1,582 in taxes. That's basically a 15.8 percent tax rate on that last $10,000 in income (and that includes added taxes on Social Security benefits). So their marginal rate seems to be around 15 percent, though they would nominally be in the 28 percent bracket.

What's the big deal? Well, in that particular case, it means the couple has $1,300 a year more than they thought they had. If you worked your way backwards through all of the retirement-income-needs calculations that most planners do, you'd find this reduces the couple's necessary savings.

Here's an example, done on a financial calculator. If you expect that you are going to have to pull $500 a month out of your tax-deferred retirement account (in today's dollars), and it will be taxed at a 28 percent rate, and you're 20 years away from retirement and expect to be retired for 20 years, you'll need to save $82,000, which you can do by saving $124 a month for the next 20 years.

If, instead, your post-retirement tax rate is really only 15 percent, you can shave your total savings to $65,353 and your monthly set-aside to $97 and still have enough to get $500 a month after taxes out of your account.
In most cases, the marginal rate might be even lower than 15 percent because most retirees are not earning as much as the affluent couple mentioned above.
T. Rowe Price, which is a mutual fund leader in providing educational materials to interested investors, is redoing its retirement planning software to take new tax facts into consideration.
You can contact the company at 800-225-5132 to order their printed retirement planners and find out when the software will become available.
